movements.name: Ab Wheel Rollout
movements.variant: Kneeling ab-wheel rollout emphasizing trunk anti-extension while the shoulders flex overhead.
movements.description: Start kneeling with the wheel under the shoulders, brace the ribs down toward the pelvis, roll forward only as far as the trunk can stay controlled without sagging, then pull the wheel back under the shoulders while keeping the hips and ribs connected.

hypertrophy.rationale: Good abdominal loading, but the movement is usually limited by bracing skill and shoulder position more than simple local hypertrophy progression.

strength.rationale: Strong trunk anti-extension strength signal, but not a high-load whole-body strength anchor.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build trunk and shoulder tolerance when range is controlled, but poor scaling can irritate the low back or shoulders.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Useful bracing transfer, but the kneeling rollout is not a gait, sprint, throw, or loaded carry pattern.

control.rationale: Very high motor-control demand from anti-extension, pelvic/rib position, shoulder flexion, and eccentric range control.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Efficient trunk stimulus when scaled well, but shoulder and low-back compensation can add unrelated fatigue.

setup.rationale: Requires only an ab wheel and floor space, with little adjustment.

ease.rationale: Hard to perform well because range, spinal position, shoulder control, and return mechanics are easy to lose.

progression.rationale: Progression is possible through range and reps, but load is indirect and hard to quantify.

support.rationale: Minimal external support; the user self-stabilizes trunk and shoulders throughout.

primary.name: Rectus abdominis
primary.evidenceShort: Power Wheel rollout studies show high rectus activation.
primary.evidence: Power Wheel rollout and similar abdominal-device EMG studies report high upper and lower rectus abdominis activation.

primary.name: External oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Rollout/Ab-Slide evidence shows high external-oblique activation.
primary.evidence: Abdominal rollout and Ab-Slide evidence supports external oblique as a high-activation trunk-control target.

secondary.name: Internal oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured abdominal-device activation supports a meaningful role.
secondary.evidence: Power Wheel and Ab-Slide evidence reports high internal oblique activation across nontraditional abdominal exercises, supporting a secondary trunk-stability role.

support.name: Latissimus dorsi
support.evidenceShort: Shoulder-extension support measured in Power Wheel exercise family.
support.evidence: Power Wheel abdominal exercise evidence measured latissimus dorsi activity, consistent with shoulder and trunk support during rollouts.

evidence.verdict: Kneeling ab wheel rollout: rectus abdominis and external oblique primary; internal oblique secondary; latissimus dorsi support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation; it does not prove hypertrophy, mechanical tension, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Kneeling versus standing, rollout distance, spinal position, shoulder range, wheel design, and tempo change difficulty and emphasis.
evidence.summary: The ab wheel rollout is classified as a trunk anti-extension movement with high abdominal activation and meaningful shoulder-girdle support demand.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The movement should be scaled by range of motion because compensation can shift load from the abdominal wall to the lumbar spine or shoulders.
evidence.limitations: The strongest direct evidence uses Power Wheel or Ab-Slide equipment rather than every commercial wheel design. Standing rollouts should be a separate, harder variant.

studies.type: Traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Power Wheel roll-out, pike, and knee-up were among the highest abdominal-activation exercises and also activated extraneous musculature.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Babb E, DeWitt R, et al. Electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Physical Therapy. 2006;86(5):656-671.
studies.relevance: Direct Power Wheel rollout-family EMG evidence for rectus abdominis, obliques, latissimus dorsi, and interpretation limits.

studies.finding: Ab-Slide produced high rectus abdominis, external oblique, and internal oblique activation.
studies.citation: Youdas JW, Guck BR, Hebrink RC, Rugotzke JD, Madson TJ, Hollman JH. An electromyographic analysis of the Ab-Slide exercise, abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust, and side bridge in healthy young adults. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2008;22(6):1939-1946. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818745bf.
studies.relevance: Close rollout-style abdominal-device evidence for abdominal wall activation.

movements.name: Bar Bench Press
movements.variant: Flat barbell bench press, treated as a free-weight horizontal pressing pattern.
movements.description: Lie flat with eyes under the racked bar, feet planted, shoulder blades set against the bench, and hands slightly wider than shoulder width; unrack by moving the bar over the shoulder joints with wrists stacked over elbows, lower under control toward the lower chest or sternum with elbows roughly 45-70 degrees from the torso, then press back up without losing shoulder position.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong pectoralis and triceps loading, but the fixed bar path and powerlifting-style setup make it less purely hypertrophy-biased than freer or more targeted press options.

strength.rationale: Elite upper-body strength anchor because heavy bilateral loading, stable setup, and precise barbell increments map cleanly to force expression.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides some shoulder and elbow exposure, but it is not primarily a joint-resilience drill and can be limiting for irritated shoulders when technique, range, or volume are poorly matched.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Low transfer to athletic coordination because the body is supine, bilateral, externally braced, and the movement path is narrow.

control.rationale: Requires bar path and bracing control, but balance, unilateral control, locomotion, and whole-body coordination demands are limited.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Useful pressing stimulus, but heavy barbell loading, warm-up sets, spotter/rack demands, and shoulder/triceps fatigue reduce stimulus-per-recovery efficiency.

setup.rationale: Requires a bench, rack, bar, plates, safety setup or spotter judgment, and repeatable rack height. It is common but not low-friction.

ease.rationale: The pattern is familiar, but safe repeatable execution requires bar path, scapular position, grip, arch, touch point, and unrack control.

progression.rationale: One of the cleanest progressive-overload movements because load, reps, range, and barbell increments are directly trackable.

support.rationale: The bench supports the torso, but the bar path is free and the lifter must stabilize shoulders, elbows, wrists, and trunk tension under heavy load.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: High activation in seated/horizontal press EMG.
primary.evidence: Surface electromyography studies of seated chest press and horizontal bench press variants consistently measure substantial pectoralis major activation during horizontal pressing.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Meaningful press assist; angle/path sensitive.
secondary.evidence: Anterior deltoid activity is repeatedly measured during horizontal pressing; its contribution varies with bench angle, grip, and handle path.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Elbow-extension contributor; grip/path sensitive.
secondary.evidence: Triceps brachii contributes to elbow extension during pressing, with activation influenced by grip width and movement variant.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Scapulothoracic support; not primary chest target.
support.evidence: Serratus anterior activity has been reported in bench press and chest press comparisons and is best classified here as scapulothoracic support rather than a primary hypertrophy target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Glenohumeral stabilization during pressing.
support.evidence: Bench press research demonstrates direction-specific rotator cuff recruitment consistent with glenohumeral stabilization during pressing.

evidence.verdict: Flat barbell horizontal press: pectoralis major primary; anterior deltoid and triceps secondary; serratus anterior and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Grip width, bar path, arch, bench angle, and equipment change emphasis; dumbbell and machine versions should be separate movements.
evidence.summary: The flat bar bench press is classified as a free-weight horizontal pressing exercise. The best available evidence supports pectoralis major as the primary target, with clinically meaningful anterior deltoid and triceps brachii contribution. Serratus anterior and rotator cuff involvement is classified as shoulder and scapulothoracic support rather than as a primary hypertrophy target.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation during a specific exercise condition. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: Bar bench press mechanics differ by grip width, touch point, arch, range of motion, tempo, load, and bench angle. Machine and dumbbell pressing evidence is used only when it is biomechanically close to the flat barbell horizontal press pattern.

studies.shortCitation: Muyor et al., J Hum Kinet, 2023
studies.finding: Seated chest press/bench variants measured pec regions, anterior deltoid, and triceps.
studies.citation: Muyor JM, Rodriguez-Ridao D, Oliva-Lozano JM. Comparison of Muscle Activity between the Horizontal Bench Press and the Seated Chest Press Exercises Using Several Grips. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2023;87:23-34. doi:10.5114/jhk/161468.
studies.relevance: Directly compared seated chest press grips with horizontal bench press grips and measured pectoralis major regions, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii.

studies.type: Systematic review of bench press EMG
studies.finding: Bench press EMG literature supports pec/triceps dominance and key interpretation limits.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Golas A, Blazek D, Maszczyk A, Wilk M, Pietraszewski P, Petr M, Uhlir P, Zajac A. A systematic review of surface electromyography analyses of the bench press movement task. PLOS ONE. 2017;12(2):e0171632. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0171632.
studies.relevance: Summarizes bench press EMG evidence and supports pectoralis major and triceps brachii as dominant contributors in the movement family.

studies.finding: Bench angle shifts pec, anterior deltoid, and triceps activation.
studies.citation: Rodriguez-Ridao D, Antequera-Vique JA, Martin-Fuentes I, Muyor JM. Effect of Five Bench Inclinations on the Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, and Triceps Brachii during the Bench Press Exercise. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2020;17(19):7339. doi:10.3390/ijerph17197339.
studies.relevance: Shows how bench angle changes pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii activation in the close horizontal/incline pressing family.

studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment is direction-specific during bench press and row tasks.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Supports rotator cuff involvement as direction-specific shoulder stabilization during bench press tasks.

studies.type: Chest press lever machine EMG and scapular kinematics
studies.finding: Chest press lever machine data includes pec, anterior deltoid, serratus, and scapular kinematics.
studies.citation: Borges E, Dalla H, Mastandrea L, Nunes S, Santarem J. Comparative evaluation of muscular activation and scapular kinematics in a chest press lever machine and a barbell bench press. Journal of Physical Education and Sport. 2019;19:912-916. doi:10.7752/jpes.2019.s3131.
studies.relevance: Compared a chest press lever machine with barbell bench press and measured pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and serratus anterior with scapular kinematics.

movements.name: Bulgarian Split Squat
movements.variant: Rear-foot-elevated split squat with the front leg doing most of the work; external load may be held at the sides but the movement is not machine-guided.
movements.description: Stand in a split stance with the rear foot elevated on a bench, keep most pressure through the front foot, lower under control until the front knee and hip are deeply flexed, then drive through the front foot to stand while keeping the knee tracking over the toes and the pelvis steady.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong quad and glute stimulus through long range, but balance and discomfort can limit loading before target muscles are fully exhausted.

strength.rationale: Builds unilateral leg force well, but absolute loading and force expression are less clean than bilateral barbell or machine patterns.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful knee, hip, ankle, and tendon tolerance stimulus through deep single-leg ranges when progressed gradually.

athletic_transfer.rationale: High carryover potential from unilateral support, hip-knee-ankle coordination, pelvic control, and force production from one leg.

control.rationale: High motor-control demand from front-foot balance, pelvis control, knee tracking, trunk position, and rear-foot constraint.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Good local stimulus, but balance, breathing, discomfort, and unilateral set volume create meaningful systemic and coordination fatigue.

setup.rationale: Requires a bench or platform, reproducible stance distance, and sometimes dumbbell setup; friction is moderate.

ease.rationale: Technically demanding because stance length, rear-foot height, depth, balance, pelvis position, and knee path are easy to vary.

progression.rationale: Progression is possible with reps and load, but measurement is noisy because stance length, depth, balance, and rear-foot placement change difficulty.

support.rationale: Very little external support; the bench constrains the rear foot but the working leg and trunk self-stabilize the movement.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: RFESS EMG shows high vastus lateralis activity.
primary.evidence: Rear-foot-elevated split squat evidence reports substantial vastus lateralis activation, especially in the bottom portion of the repetition, supporting quadriceps as a primary target.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: RFESS and Bulgarian squat studies measure meaningful gluteal activation.
primary.evidence: Rear-foot-elevated split squat and Bulgarian squat studies measure gluteus maximus activation and support a primary hip-extension role, with emphasis changing by depth and trunk position.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured posterior-chain assistant in RFESS.
secondary.evidence: RFESS evidence measured medial and lateral hamstring activation; the role is meaningful but secondary to the stronger knee-extension and hip-extension targets.

support.name: Gluteus medius
support.evidenceShort: Hip-abductor control demand in lunge/single-leg patterns.
support.evidence: Bulgarian squat and related single-leg/lunge EMG evidence supports gluteus medius involvement for frontal-plane hip and pelvic control.

support.name: Trunk stabilizers
support.evidenceShort: Trunk position changes lunge-family muscle activation.
support.evidence: Lunge-family evidence shows trunk position changes muscular activation; trunk stabilizers are listed as support because the unsupported split stance requires bracing and postural control.

evidence.verdict: Rear-foot-elevated split squat: quadriceps and gluteus maximus primary; hamstrings secondary; gluteus medius and trunk stabilizers support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Rear-foot height, stance length, trunk angle, load position, depth, balance, and suspension or instability devices materially change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The Bulgarian split squat is classified as an unsupported unilateral lower-body compound movement. Current evidence supports quadriceps and gluteus maximus as the main visible targets, with hamstrings contributing as assistants and gluteus medius/trunk stabilizers supporting single-leg control.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is condition-specific and should be interpreted alongside joint action, range of motion, load, and technique.
evidence.limitations: The entry assumes a stable rear-foot-elevated split squat. Suspended, vibration, unstable-surface, Smith-machine, barbell, and heavy dumbbell variants should be split later if the app needs variant-specific scoring.

studies.finding: RFESS produced high vastus lateralis activation and measured gluteus maximus plus medial and lateral hamstrings.
studies.citation: McCurdy K, Walker J, Kelly C, Polinski M. Hip and Knee Extensor Activation During the Hip Thrust and Rear-Foot-Elevated Split Squat in Trained Females. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2021;35(5):1201-1207. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000004035.
studies.relevance: Direct RFESS EMG source for quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and hamstrings.

studies.finding: Bulgarian squat variants changed lower-limb muscle activity under vibration, suspension, and unstable-surface conditions.
studies.citation: Aguilera-Castells J, Buscà B, Arboix-Alió J, et al. Muscle activity of Bulgarian squat. Effects of additional vibration, suspension and unstable surface. PLOS ONE. 2019;14(8):e0221710. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0221710.
studies.relevance: Direct Bulgarian squat evidence for muscle activation and instability-sensitive control demand.

studies.type: Hip muscle activation in lunge and single-leg tasks
studies.shortCitation: Boudreau et al., J Sport Rehabil, 2009
studies.finding: Lunge, single-leg squat, and step-up tasks produced meaningful hip-muscle activation.
studies.citation: Boudreau SN, Dwyer MK, Mattacola CG, Lattermann C, Uhl TL, McKeon JM. Hip-muscle activation during the lunge, single-leg squat, and step-up-and-over exercises. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2009;18(1):91-103. doi:10.1123/jsr.18.1.91.
studies.relevance: Close single-leg/lunge-family source supporting gluteus medius support classification.

studies.finding: Trunk position during lunge exercises changed muscular activation in trained women.
studies.citation: Bezerra ES, et al. Influence of Trunk Position during Three Lunge Exercises on Muscular Activation in Trained Women. International Journal of Exercise Science. 2021;14(1):202-214. doi:10.70252/IGJM9937.
studies.relevance: Close lunge-family evidence for trunk-position sensitivity and support-role limitations.

movements.name: Dumbbell Bench Press
movements.variant: Flat dumbbell bench press, treated as an independent free-weight horizontal pressing pattern.
movements.description: Sit at the end of a flat bench with matching dumbbells on the thighs, lie back while guiding the weights to shoulder level, set the feet and shoulder blades, lower with wrists stacked over elbows until the chest is loaded without losing shoulder position, then press the dumbbells up and slightly together under control.

hypertrophy.rationale: High chest stimulus with independent arm paths and useful range of motion, making hypertrophy a main positive dimension.

strength.rationale: Builds pressing strength well, but absolute loading and measurement precision are lower than barbell bench because each dumbbell must be positioned and stabilized independently.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can train shoulder tolerance through a freer path, but it is not primarily a resilience drill and can become demanding at the bottom range.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Some transfer from independent limb control, but the supine supported position keeps sport-like coordination demand low.

control.rationale: Meaningful control demand from independent dumbbells, but the bench removes balance, locomotion, and most whole-body coordination.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Strong local stimulus, but setup, stabilizer demand, and heavy dumbbell handling reduce efficiency compared with guided chest work.

setup.rationale: Needs a bench and matched dumbbells, with extra friction as weights get heavy or crowded.

ease.rationale: Simple conceptually, but safe heavy reps require independent arm control, shoulder positioning, and getting dumbbells into and out of position.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are trackable, but dumbbell jumps are often coarse and heavy setup can limit progression before the target muscles do.

support.rationale: The torso is bench-supported, but each arm stabilizes a separate free load, so external support is modest.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: Direct DBP and bench-press EMG support major chest involvement.
primary.evidence: Dumbbell bench press studies measure pectoralis major activity during the horizontal press, and bench-press EMG review evidence supports pectoralis major as a dominant mover in the movement family.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured DBP contributor; path and depth sensitive.
secondary.evidence: Anterior deltoid is directly measured during dumbbell bench press and close bench-press variants; its contribution is meaningful but generally secondary to the intended chest target.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Elbow-extension contributor in DBP and bench press.
secondary.evidence: Dumbbell bench press EMG studies record triceps brachii activity, and the bench-press EMG literature identifies triceps brachii as a major contributor to the elbow-extension component of pressing.

support.name: Biceps brachii
support.evidenceShort: Independent dumbbells increase antagonist/stabilizer demand.
support.evidence: Direct dumbbell bench press comparisons report biceps brachii activity consistent with antagonist and stabilizing demand when controlling two independent dumbbells.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Scapulothoracic support during horizontal pressing.
support.evidence: Bench and chest-press comparison evidence includes serratus anterior activity with scapular kinematics; for dumbbell pressing this is classified as scapulothoracic support rather than a primary hypertrophy target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Glenohumeral stabilization during free pressing.
support.evidence: Bench press research demonstrates direction-specific rotator cuff recruitment consistent with glenohumeral stabilization; independent dumbbell paths make this a support classification.

evidence.verdict: Flat dumbbell horizontal press: pectoralis major primary; anterior deltoid and triceps secondary; biceps brachii, serratus anterior, and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Dumbbell path, depth, grip angle, load, bench angle, shoulder range, and start/finish handling can shift emphasis; incline, neutral-grip, and machine versions should be separate movements.
evidence.summary: The flat dumbbell bench press is classified as an independent free-weight horizontal pressing exercise. Direct dumbbell press evidence supports pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, triceps brachii, and biceps brachii involvement. Pectoralis major is the primary target, anterior deltoid and triceps brachii are secondary movers, and biceps brachii is included as support because independent dumbbells increase antagonist/stabilizer demand.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation during a specific exercise condition. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: Dumbbell bench press studies differ in load prescription, normalization method, range of motion, grip, participant training status, and whether the comparison condition is barbell, Smith machine, cable, or fly variation. Scapular and rotator cuff support roles are inferred from close pressing-family evidence rather than direct dumbbell-only measurements.

studies.shortCitation: Rosa et al., Int J Strength Cond, 2024

studies.relevance: Directly measured pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, biceps brachii, and triceps brachii during dumbbell bench press in resistance-trained participants.

studies.type: Dumbbell, barbell, and Smith machine bench press EMG
studies.finding: Compared DBP, barbell, and Smith machine bench press over multiple sets and measured pec, anterior deltoid, biceps, and triceps.
studies.citation: Farias D de A, Willardson JM, Paz GA, Bezerra E de S, Miranda H. studies.relevance: Directly supports DBP muscle-role classification and the stabilizer demand distinction between dumbbell and bar/machine modalities.

studies.finding: Compared Smith machine, barbell, and dumbbell chest press 1RM and EMG under different stability requirements.
studies.citation: Saeterbakken AH, van den Tillaar R, Fimland MS. A comparison of muscle activity and 1-RM strength of three chest-press exercises with different stability requirements. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2011;29(5):533-538. doi:10.1080/02640414.2010.543916.
studies.relevance: Directly compares dumbbell pressing with more stable press modes and supports the support/stability scoring and biceps support classification.

studies.finding: Measured pectoralis major and anterior deltoid activity during barbell bench press, dumbbell bench press, and dumbbell fly.
studies.citation: Welsch EA, Bird M, Mayhew JL. Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major and Anterior Deltoid Muscles During Three Upper-Body Lifts. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2005;19(2):449-452. doi:10.1519/14513.1.
studies.relevance: Directly includes dumbbell bench press and supports pectoralis major and anterior deltoid classification.

studies.type: Systematic review of bench press EMG
studies.finding: Bench press EMG literature supports pec/triceps dominance and highlights stability, intensity, phase, and technique limits.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Golas A, Blazek D, Maszczyk A, Wilk M, Pietraszewski P, Petr M, Uhlir P, Zajac A. A systematic review of surface electromyography analyses of the bench press movement task. PLOS ONE. 2017;12(2):e0171632. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0171632.
studies.relevance: Provides movement-family context for pectoralis major, triceps brachii, anterior deltoid, and stability-condition interpretation.

studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment is direction-specific during bench press and row tasks.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Supports rotator cuff involvement as shoulder stabilization during pressing tasks.

studies.type: Chest press lever machine EMG and scapular kinematics
studies.finding: Chest press lever machine data includes pec, anterior deltoid, serratus, and scapular kinematics.
studies.citation: Borges E, Dalla H, Mastandrea L, Nunes S, Santarem J. Comparative evaluation of muscular activation and scapular kinematics in a chest press lever machine and a barbell bench press. Journal of Physical Education and Sport. 2019;19:912-916. doi:10.7752/jpes.2019.s3131.
studies.relevance: Supports serratus anterior as scapulothoracic support in the close horizontal pressing family.

movements.name: Dumbbell Walking Lunge
movements.variant: Alternating dumbbell walking lunge with two free weights held at the sides.
movements.description: Stand tall holding matching dumbbells at the sides, step forward into a long enough stride to lower under control without the front heel lifting, descend until the rear knee approaches the floor, then drive through the lead foot and bring the trailing leg forward into the next step. Alternate legs while keeping the torso controlled, the front knee tracking over the foot, and each step length consistent.

hypertrophy.rationale: Meaningful lower-body hypertrophy stimulus, especially for quads and glutes, but balance, breathing, and locomotion can limit target-muscle loading.

strength.rationale: Builds unilateral force capacity, but load expression is less clean than bilateral barbell or machine patterns.

joint_resilience.rationale: Excellent knee, hip, ankle, and connective-tissue capacity builder when progressed well because it loads long ranges, single-leg support, and repeated deceleration.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Elite transfer dimension because it combines loaded gait, unilateral support, hip-knee-ankle coordination, trunk control, and forward force transfer.

control.rationale: Very high control demand from dynamic balance, step length, pelvis control, trunk position, grip, and repeated single-leg transitions.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low efficiency for isolated stimulus because breathing, grip, balance, locomotion, and large-muscle systemic fatigue accumulate quickly.

setup.rationale: Requires only dumbbells and floor space, but usable lane length, turning, matched loads, and heavy dumbbell pickup add friction.

ease.rationale: Technically and physically demanding: stride length, knee tracking, balance, depth, torso angle, and continuous stepping are all easy to vary unintentionally.

progression.rationale: Progression is possible through load, steps, and reps, but measurement is noisy because stride length, lane length, balance, and fatigue alter difficulty.

support.rationale: Almost no external support: the user stabilizes each step through the foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, trunk, and grip.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: High VM/VL/RF activity in loaded forward and walking lunges.
primary.evidence: Direct dumbbell forward-lunge-with-stride and walking-lunge studies report high vastus medialis and vastus lateralis activation, with rectus femoris also measured; lunge studies consistently place quadriceps among the main knee-extension contributors.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: High hip-extension demand in loaded lunge evidence.
primary.evidence: The closest two-dumbbell forward-lunge-with-stride study reported high gluteus maximus activity during ascent, and loaded anterior-lunge biomechanics identify the lunge as hip-extensor dominant. This supports gluteus maximus as a primary hip-extension target, while recognizing that step length and trunk angle shift emphasis.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured moderate posterior-chain contribution.
secondary.evidence: Walking-lunge and dumbbell forward-lunge studies measure biceps femoris and semitendinosus activity; activation is meaningful but generally below the strongest quadriceps and gluteal signals, so hamstrings are classified as secondary rather than primary.

support.name: Gluteus medius
support.evidenceShort: High frontal-plane and pelvic-control demand in walking lunges.
support.evidence: Walking-lunge evidence reports substantial gluteus medius activity, and the dynamic walking or with-stride component increases demand compared with more static lunge patterns. It is listed as support because its main role is pelvic, hip, and frontal-plane control rather than sagittal-plane propulsion.

support.name: Adductor longus
support.evidenceShort: Moderate activation in dumbbell forward-lunge variants.
support.evidence: The closest bilateral-dumbbell forward-lunge study measured moderate adductor longus activity, especially with longer step conditions, supporting a visible support role for hip and stance control.

support.name: Gastrocnemius
support.evidenceShort: Measured ankle/stance contribution during loaded lunges.
support.evidence: Dumbbell forward-lunge evidence measured moderate gastrocnemius activation, and external-load biomechanics show ankle work rising with load. This supports a calf support role for ankle control and forward stepping rather than a primary hypertrophy target.

support.name: Trunk stabilizers
support.evidenceShort: Dumbbell lunge loading changes trunk muscle activation.
support.evidence: A lunge load-distribution EMG study measured erector spinae, external oblique, rectus abdominis, and latissimus dorsi responses to dumbbell loading positions; this supports a trunk stabilization role, especially when dumbbells challenge posture and anti-rotation.

evidence.verdict: Alternating dumbbell walking lunge: quadriceps and gluteus maximus primary; hamstrings secondary; gluteus medius, adductor longus, gastrocnemius, and trunk stabilizers support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Continuous walking, push-back forward lunges, step length, trunk angle, dumbbell load, and dumbbell carrying position all change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The dumbbell walking lunge is classified as a dynamic unilateral lower-body compound exercise. The best evidence includes a direct dumbbell forward-lunge-with-stride EMG study using two dumbbells, walking-lunge EMG studies using load-carrying variants, forward-lunge EMG studies, and loaded lunge biomechanics. These sources support quadriceps and gluteus maximus as the main prime movers, hamstrings as meaningful assistants, and gluteus medius, adductor longus, gastrocnemius, and trunk stabilizers as control or support contributors.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation in a given technique and load condition. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, training adaptation, soreness, joint safety, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: Exact evidence for a continuous alternating two-dumbbell walking lunge is limited. The strongest exact walking-lunge studies used walking lunges with dumbbell carrying-position variations or examined associations with strength ratios, while the strongest bilateral-dumbbell source used forward lunges with a stride and a push back to the start. Step length, trunk lean, stride continuity, load, fatigue, footwear, and participant training status can materially alter muscle activity and joint loading.

studies.type: Dumbbell forward-lunge stride and step-length EMG
studies.finding: With two dumbbells and 12RM loads, forward lunges with stride showed high to very high quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and gluteus medius activity, with moderate hamstrings, gastrocnemius, and adductor longus activity.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Thompson IS, Asuncion R, Bravo J, Chang T, Fournier T, Garcia H, Hockenbery E, Nagasawa K, Ozor J, Snoeberger H, Wilk KE, Bizzini M. Effects of Step Length and Stride Variation During Forward Lunges on Lower-Extremity Muscle Activity. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2025;10(1):42. doi:10.3390/jfmk10010042.
studies.relevance: Closest bilateral-dumbbell source: participants held one dumbbell in each hand and performed forward lunge variations with and without a stride while lower-extremity EMG was recorded.

studies.finding: Compared dumbbell carrying positions during split squats and walking lunges, measuring gluteus medius, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, and biceps femoris.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Lehnert M, Zaatar AMZ, Svoboda Z, Xaverova Z. Does the Dumbbell-Carrying Position Change the Muscle Activity in Split Squats and Walking Lunges? Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2015;29(11):3177-3187. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000000976.
studies.relevance: Directly includes walking lunges and dumbbell loading, but the loading arrangement studied carrying position rather than the exact bilateral-at-sides assumption.

studies.finding: Resistance-trained men performed walking lunges and split squats at 5RM; walking lunges produced higher gluteus medius activity than split squats and were recommended when gluteus medius or vastus medialis strengthening is the aim.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Tufano JJ, Lehnert M, Golas A, Zaatar A, Xaverova Z, Maszczyk A. Hip abductors and thigh muscles strength ratios and their relation to electromyography amplitude during split squat and walking lunge exercises. Acta Gymnica. 2015;45(2):51-59. doi:10.5507/ag.2015.011.
studies.relevance: Direct walking-lunge EMG evidence for vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, biceps femoris, and gluteus medius in trained men.

studies.finding: In forward lunges, vastus lateralis and vastus medialis showed the highest activation, followed by gluteus medius and gluteus maximus, then rectus femoris and biceps femoris.
studies.citation: Muyor JM, Martin-Fuentes I, Rodriguez-Ridao D, Antequera-Vique JA. Electromyographic activity in the gluteus medius, gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and rectus femoris during the Monopodal Squat, Forward Lunge and Lateral Step-Up exercises. PLOS ONE. 2020;15(4):e0230841. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0230841.
studies.relevance: Close lunge-family EMG evidence measuring key quadriceps, gluteal, and hamstring muscles during forward lunges at 60% of 5RM.

studies.shortCitation: Riemann et al., J Athl Train, 2012
studies.finding: Anterior lunges with added external load were hip-extensor dominant kinetically; adding load increased mechanical work mainly at the hip and ankle.
studies.citation: Riemann BL, Lapinski S, Smith L, Davies G. Biomechanical Analysis of the Anterior Lunge During 4 External-Load Conditions. Journal of Athletic Training. 2012;47(4):372-378. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-47.4.16.
studies.relevance: Biomechanical evidence for hip and ankle joint demand under external loading in a close anterior-lunge pattern.

studies.shortCitation: Wu et al., J Sport Rehabil, 2020
studies.finding: Loaded lunges showed higher activation than unloaded lunges; quadriceps and hamstring activities were higher in lunge than squat, and lunge muscle activation did not differ meaningfully among the tested loading devices.
studies.citation: Wu HW, Tsai CF, Liang KH, Chang YW. Effect of Loading Devices on Muscle Activation in Squat and Lunge. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2020;29(2):200-205. doi:10.1123/jsr.2018-0182.
studies.relevance: Supports the interpretation that loading increases lunge muscle activity and that dumbbell loading is a reasonable free-weight lunge condition.

studies.type: Dumbbell forward-lunge EMG load and contraction comparison
studies.shortCitation: Jakobsen et al., Hum Mov Sci, 2013
studies.finding: Standardized forward lunges performed with dumbbells and elastic resistance showed load-dependent EMG increases; quadriceps and gluteus EMG increased at flexed knee positions.
studies.citation: Jakobsen MD, Sundstrup E, Andersen CH, Aagaard P, Andersen LL. Muscle activity during leg strengthening exercise using free weights and elastic resistance: Effects of ballistic vs controlled contractions. Human Movement Science. 2013;32(1):65-78. doi:10.1016/j.humov.2012.07.002.
studies.relevance: Directly includes dumbbell forward lunges and supports load-dependent quadriceps and gluteal activation in a close free-weight lunge pattern.

studies.finding: Dumbbell lunge load placement changed erector spinae, external oblique, rectus abdominis, and latissimus dorsi activation, supporting trunk stabilization demands.
studies.citation: Lopez-de-Celis C, Labata-Lezaun N, Romani-Sanchez S, Gasso-Villarejo S, Garcia-Ribell E, Rodriguez-Sanz J, Perez-Bellmunt A. Effect of Load Distribution on Trunk Muscle Activity with Lunge Exercises in Amateur Athletes: Cross-Sectional Study. Healthcare. 2023;11(6):916. doi:10.3390/healthcare11060916.
studies.relevance: Direct lunge evidence for trunk muscle support under dumbbell loading arrangements.

studies.finding: In novice men, dumbbell-loaded lunge squats showed smaller center-of-pressure displacement and high hip-joint moment changes compared with other loading conditions.
studies.citation: Gao L, Lu Z, Liang M, Baker JS, Gu Y. Influence of Different Load Conditions on Lower Extremity Biomechanics during the Lunge Squat in Novice Men. Bioengineering. 2022;9(7):272. doi:10.3390/bioengineering9070272.
studies.relevance: Supports dumbbell-loading rating interpretation for stability, hip demand, and load-condition limitations in a close lunge-squat task.

movements.name: Ground Oblique Crunch
movements.variant: Bodyweight floor crunch biased toward trunk rotation or lateral flexion for the obliques.
movements.description: Lie on the floor with the knees bent, brace lightly, curl the ribs toward the opposite hip or side-crunch toward one hip without yanking the neck, pause with the trunk shortened, then lower under control before repeating on the same side or alternating.

hypertrophy.rationale: Can train the obliques locally, but load is light and progression is limited.

strength.rationale: Low strength signal because it is mostly bodyweight trunk flexion with poor external loading.

joint_resilience.rationale: Low joint-resilience value; repeated spinal flexion/rotation is not broadly useful as a resilience anchor.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Low transfer because it lacks standing force transfer, anti-rotation demand, or integrated limb coordination.

control.rationale: Some trunk-position control is required, but the floor and short range make coordination demands low.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low systemic fatigue and quick local abdominal stimulus, though the stimulus ceiling is low.

setup.rationale: Almost no setup: floor space only.

ease.rationale: Easy to understand, though users can compensate with neck pulling or hip flexion.

progression.rationale: Difficult to progressively overload precisely without changing to a cable, machine, or loaded variation.

support.rationale: The floor supports the body and removes balance demand.

primary.name: External oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Crunch/side-bridge EMG supports oblique activation.
primary.evidence: Crunch and side-bridge EMG evidence measures external oblique activity; the oblique-biased crunch is classified as targeting this role directly.

primary.name: Internal oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Crunch/side-bridge EMG supports internal-oblique activation.
primary.evidence: Abdominal crunch, side bridge, and related abdominal EMG evidence measure internal oblique activity, supporting a primary oblique role for this variant.

secondary.name: Rectus abdominis
secondary.evidenceShort: Crunch evidence shows rectus activity, but this variant is oblique-biased.
secondary.evidence: Crunch EMG evidence reports substantial rectus abdominis activity; it is secondary here because the movement is intentionally oblique-biased.

evidence.verdict: Ground oblique crunch: external and internal oblique primary; rectus abdominis secondary; no separate support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Side-lying versus supine rotation, hand position, range, tempo, neck compensation, and hip flexion change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The ground oblique crunch is classified as a low-setup trunk flexion or rotation movement. Evidence is from the abdominal crunch and side-bridge family rather than a single standardized oblique-crunch protocol, so classification is conservative.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: This is a low-friction accessory movement, not a high-load core progression anchor.
evidence.limitations: The exact phrase 'oblique crunch' covers several setups. Cable wood chops, cable crunches, side planks, and weighted oblique crunches should be separate entries.

studies.type: Commercial and common abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Crunch and abdominal-device exercises activated rectus abdominis plus external and internal obliques.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, McTaggart MSC, Fricklas EJ, et al. An electromyographic analysis of commercial and common abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2006;36(2):45-57. doi:10.2519/jospt.2006.36.2.45.
studies.relevance: Common abdominal exercise EMG source for rectus abdominis and oblique activation.

studies.finding: Compared Ab-Slide, abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust, and side bridge using rectus abdominis and oblique EMG.
studies.citation: Youdas JW, Guck BR, Hebrink RC, Rugotzke JD, Madson TJ, Hollman JH. An electromyographic analysis of the Ab-Slide exercise, abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust, and side bridge in healthy young adults. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2008;22(6):1939-1946. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818745bf.
studies.relevance: Close evidence for external oblique, internal oblique, and rectus abdominis activation during accessible floor core exercises.

movements.name: Hanging Leg Raise
movements.variant: Hanging leg or knee raise from a pull-up bar or straps, emphasizing controlled hip flexion and posterior pelvic tilt.
movements.description: Hang from a bar or straps with the shoulders controlled, brace the ribs down, raise the knees or legs by flexing the hips and curling the pelvis upward, pause without swinging, then lower under control until the trunk is stable again.

hypertrophy.rationale: Useful abdominal and hip-flexor loading, but grip, swing control, and hip flexion often limit local hypertrophy progression.

strength.rationale: Good trunk and hip-flexion strength signal, especially when done with posterior pelvic tilt and long lever control.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build shoulder hanging tolerance and anterior-core control, but it is not a broad joint-resilience anchor.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Moderate transfer to hanging, climbing, and trunk-control tasks, but low direct transfer to loaded lower-body or gait patterns.

control.rationale: High motor-control demand from grip/hang stability, swing suppression, hip flexion, pelvic curl, and eccentric lowering.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Can be effective, but grip, shoulder, and hip-flexor fatigue often leak into the stimulus.

setup.rationale: Requires a bar or straps and enough clearance, but little loading setup.

ease.rationale: Difficult to repeat cleanly because swinging and hip-flexor dominance can hide poor trunk control.

progression.rationale: Progression can use reps, knee-to-leg leverage, tempo, or load, but the main difficulty variable is hard to quantify.

support.rationale: Almost no external support; the body hangs freely and self-stabilizes.

primary.name: Rectus abdominis
primary.evidenceShort: Hanging knee-up evidence shows high rectus activation.
primary.evidence: Hanging knee-up EMG evidence reports high upper and lower rectus abdominis activation, supporting a primary abdominal role.

primary.name: Iliopsoas
primary.evidenceShort: Hip-flexor EMG supports primary hip-flexion role.
primary.evidence: Hanging leg raises require resisted hip flexion, and hip-flexor EMG evidence supports iliopsoas involvement in leg-raise and hip-flexion tasks.

secondary.name: External oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Hanging knee-up evidence shows high external-oblique activity.
secondary.evidence: Hanging knee-up EMG evidence reports high external oblique activity, supporting a secondary trunk-control role.

secondary.name: Internal oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Abdominal EMG supports oblique contribution.
secondary.evidence: Traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercise EMG supports internal oblique contribution during high-demand leg-raise and knee-up patterns.

support.name: Latissimus dorsi
support.evidenceShort: Hanging setup requires shoulder-girdle support.
support.evidence: Latissimus dorsi is included as support because hanging from a bar requires shoulder-girdle control while the trunk and hips move; abdominal-device evidence also measured latissimus involvement in related high-demand abdominal tasks.

evidence.verdict: Hanging leg raise: rectus abdominis and iliopsoas primary; external and internal oblique secondary; latissimus dorsi support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Knee bend, straight-leg lever length, pelvic curl, straps versus bar, swing, grip fatigue, and load change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The hanging leg raise is classified as a hanging trunk and hip-flexion exercise. Evidence supports high abdominal activation in hanging knee-up variants, with iliopsoas included from hip-flexor EMG and the movement's primary hip-flexion mechanics.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: A clean posterior pelvic tilt makes this more abdominal; a pure hip-flexion swing makes it more hip-flexor dominant.
evidence.limitations: Most direct evidence uses hanging knee-ups with straps rather than every straight-leg bar-hanging variant. Straight-leg raises, captain's-chair raises, toes-to-bar, and weighted raises should be split later if precision matters.

studies.type: Traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Hanging knee-up with straps was among the highest abdominal activation exercises for rectus abdominis and obliques.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Babb E, DeWitt R, et al. Electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Physical Therapy. 2006;86(5):656-671.
studies.relevance: Direct hanging knee-up abdominal EMG source for rectus abdominis and obliques.

studies.shortCitation: Lee et al., J Phys Ther Sci, 2016
studies.finding: Compared abdominal and lower-limb muscle activity during sit-up and leg-raise tasks.
studies.citation: Lee DK, Kang MH, Lee TS, Oh JS. Comparison of muscular activities in the abdomen and lower limbs while performing sit-up and leg-raise. Journal of Physical Therapy Science. 2016;28(2):491-494. doi:10.1589/jpts.28.491.
studies.relevance: Close leg-raise source supporting abdominal and hip-flexion interpretation.

studies.shortCitation: Czuppon et al., J Clin Med, 2024
studies.finding: Measured hip-flexor muscle activation during common rehabilitation and strength exercises.
studies.citation: Czuppon S, et al. Hip Flexor Muscle Activation During Common Rehabilitation and Strength Exercises. Journal of Clinical Medicine. 2024;13(21):6617. doi:10.3390/jcm13216617.
studies.relevance: Supports iliopsoas inclusion for the hip-flexion component.

movements.name: Incline Bar Bench Press
movements.variant: Incline barbell bench press using a fixed incline bench and a free barbell, treated as an upward-angled free-weight chest press.
movements.description: Lie back on a fixed incline bench with the eyes slightly behind the racked bar, feet planted, shoulder blades set against the pad, and hands slightly wider than shoulder width; unrack to a stacked wrist-over-elbow position, lower the bar under control toward the upper chest without letting the elbows flare excessively, then press up and slightly back toward the rack line while keeping the torso and shoulder position stable.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong upper-chest and anterior-shoulder hypertrophy stimulus, with useful overload but less flat-pec emphasis than the flat press.

strength.rationale: Strong barbell strength movement with clear loading, though absolute force is usually lower and setup is more angle-specific than flat bench.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides controlled shoulder exposure but is not a resilience-focused drill and can be shoulder-demanding for some users.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Low athletic-transfer score because the task is bilateral, supine, braced, and not coordination-rich.

control.rationale: Requires bar path and upper-body position control, but balance and whole-body coordination demands remain low.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Useful pressing stimulus but heavy setup, shoulder/triceps overlap, and warm-up demands keep efficiency moderate-low.

setup.rationale: Needs rack, bench-angle setup, bar, plates, safeties or spotter judgment, and consistent bench placement.

ease.rationale: Less automatic than flat bench because angle, touch point, shoulder position, and unrack path are harder to standardize.

progression.rationale: Excellent overload tracking because barbell load and reps are precise, with small deductions for bench-angle and rack-position variability.

support.rationale: The bench supports the torso, but the bar is still a free path and shoulder stabilization remains meaningful.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: Incline barbell EMG supports major chest involvement, especially upper pec at moderate inclines.
primary.evidence: Free-weight bench-angle EMG studies show substantial pectoralis major activity during incline bench pressing; the upper/clavicular region is emphasized around moderate incline angles, while very high inclines shift more activity toward the anterior deltoid.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Incline angle increases anterior deltoid contribution.
secondary.evidence: Bench-angle EMG studies repeatedly show anterior deltoid activity during incline pressing, with greater contribution as the bench angle rises; it is classified as secondary for a chest-focused incline press because it assists shoulder flexion and can become dominant at steeper inclines.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured elbow-extension contributor during incline pressing.
secondary.evidence: Incline and bench-press EMG studies measure triceps brachii activity during the press; its role is meaningful for elbow extension, though incline-angle studies report it as similar across angles or lower than chest and anterior deltoid activation.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Inference from close bench/chest-press scapular evidence.
support.evidence: This support role is inferred from chest-press and bench-press evidence showing serratus anterior activity with scapular kinematics; it is included as scapulothoracic support, not as a direct incline-specific hypertrophy target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Inference from bench-press shoulder-stabilization evidence.
support.evidence: This support role is inferred from bench-press research showing direction-specific rotator cuff recruitment consistent with glenohumeral stabilization under pressing loads; direct incline-only rotator cuff EMG was not found.

evidence.verdict: Incline free-bar chest press: pectoralis major primary; anterior deltoid and triceps brachii secondary; serratus anterior and rotator cuff support by marked inference from close bench-press evidence.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, pain risk, or long-term training outcome.
evidence.limitsShort: Bench angle is the main modifier: moderate inclines emphasize upper pectoralis, while steeper inclines increase anterior deltoid demand and may reduce pectoralis performance.
evidence.summary: The incline bar bench press is classified as a free-weight upward-angled chest press performed on a fixed incline bench. Direct bench-angle studies support pectoralis major as the primary target, especially the upper/clavicular region at moderate inclines. Anterior deltoid and triceps brachii are visible secondary movers because shoulder flexion and elbow extension are both required, and their activity is directly measured in incline bench research.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography should be interpreted as exercise-condition-specific muscle excitation. It does not directly measure hypertrophy, mechanical tension, joint loading, tissue tolerance, or injury probability. Ratings combine direct bench-angle evidence with explicit product judgment about setup, progression, support, and fatigue.
evidence.limitations: The exact fixed bench angle is not specified in the movement ID. Most direct evidence uses 25-45 degree incline conditions, but studies also test 60 degrees, where anterior deltoid activity becomes much more prominent. Grip width, bar touch point, load prescription, arch, rack height, spotter/safeties, tempo, and participant training status can all change the observed stimulus.

studies.finding: At 30 degrees, upper pectoralis major and anterior deltoid were among the highest measured activations; above 45 degrees, anterior deltoid increased and pectoralis performance decreased, while triceps activity was similar across inclines.
studies.citation: Rodriguez-Ridao D, Antequera-Vique JA, Martin-Fuentes I, Muyor JM. Effect of Five Bench Inclinations on the Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, and Triceps Brachii during the Bench Press Exercise. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2020;17(19):7339. doi:10.3390/ijerph17197339.
studies.relevance: Directly tested free-weight bench press at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 degrees and measured upper, middle, and lower pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii.

studies.shortCitation: Lauver et al., Eur J Sport Sci, 2016
studies.finding: Free-weight barbell bench pressing at different angles changed upper-extremity activation patterns, supporting the angle-sensitive classification of pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii.
studies.citation: Lauver JD, Cayot TE, Scheuermann BW. Influence of bench angle on upper extremity muscular activation during bench press exercise. European Journal of Sport Science. 2016;16(3):309-316. doi:10.1080/17461391.2015.1022605.
studies.relevance: Direct incline/flat/decline free-weight barbell bench-angle evidence measuring pectoralis major regions, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii.

studies.type: High-density pectoralis EMG during flat and incline bench press
studies.shortCitation: Cabral et al., Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2022
studies.finding: High-density EMG showed pectoralis major excitation shifted toward the clavicular region during a 45-degree incline bench press compared with the flat press.
studies.citation: Cabral HV, de Souza LML, de Oliveira LF, Vieira TM. Non-uniform excitation of the pectoralis major muscle during flat and inclined bench press exercises. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2022;32(2):381-390. doi:10.1111/sms.14082.
studies.relevance: Directly supports pectoralis major as the main target and clarifies regional pectoralis excitation in a 45-degree incline bench press.

studies.shortCitation: Saeterbakken et al., J Hum Kinet, 2017
studies.finding: In competitive bench press athletes, incline and decline wide-grip variations changed some arm-muscle activation and performance outcomes compared with competition-style flat pressing.
studies.citation: Saeterbakken AH, Mo DA, Scott S, Andersen V. The Effects of Bench Press Variations in Competitive Athletes on Muscle Activity and Performance. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2017;57(1):61-71. doi:10.1515/hukin-2017-0047.
studies.relevance: Close direct evidence in trained bench press athletes comparing incline, decline, and grip-width variations while measuring pectoralis major, deltoids, biceps, triceps, and latissimus dorsi.

studies.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of pectoralis EMG in bench press variants
studies.finding: The review found pectoralis major activation differs across bench-press variants and that incline benching tends to increase clavicular emphasis while reducing sternal emphasis compared with the horizontal bench press.
studies.citation: Lopez-Vivancos A, Gonzalez-Galvez N, Orquin-Castrillon FJ, de Souza Vale RG, Marcos-Pardo PJ. Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major Muscle during Traditional Bench Press and Other Variants of Pectoral Exercises: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Applied Sciences. 2023;13(8):5203. doi:10.3390/app13085203.
studies.relevance: Provides synthesis-level context for pectoralis major activation across bench-press variants, including bench inclination.

studies.type: Systematic review of bench press EMG
studies.finding: Bench press EMG literature supports pectoralis major and triceps brachii as major contributors and highlights technique, intensity, and phase-specific interpretation limits.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Golas A, Blazek D, Maszczyk A, Wilk M, Pietraszewski P, Petr M, Uhlir P, Zajac A. A systematic review of surface electromyography analyses of the bench press movement task. PLOS ONE. 2017;12(2):e0171632. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0171632.
studies.relevance: Movement-family synthesis used to support triceps classification and general EMG interpretation limits for barbell bench pressing.

studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment during bench press and row tasks was direction-specific, supporting a stabilizing shoulder role during pressing.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Close bench-press evidence used as an explicit inference for glenohumeral stabilization in the free-weight incline press.

studies.type: Chest press and barbell bench press EMG with scapular kinematics
studies.finding: Chest press lever machine and barbell bench press comparisons included serratus anterior activity and scapular kinematics.
studies.citation: Borges E, Dalla H, Mastandrea L, Nunes S, Santarem J. Comparative evaluation of muscular activation and scapular kinematics in a chest press lever machine and a barbell bench press. Journal of Physical Education and Sport. 2019;19:912-916. doi:10.7752/jpes.2019.s3131.
studies.relevance: Close horizontal pressing evidence used as an explicit inference for serratus anterior scapulothoracic support during incline pressing.

movements.name: Lying Machine Hamstring Curl
movements.variant: Prone or lying hamstring curl machine with the thighs supported and a lower-leg roller or pad applying knee-flexion resistance.
movements.description: Lie prone on the leg-curl machine with the knees aligned near the machine pivot and the roller set just above the heels. Brace lightly into the pads without letting the hips lift, flex the knees to curl the roller toward the back of the thighs, pause under control, then lower until the knees are nearly straight without losing hamstring tension.

hypertrophy.rationale: Excellent direct knee-flexion hypertrophy movement for hamstrings, though hip position is less lengthened than seated curls.

strength.rationale: Builds isolated knee-flexion force, but it does not express integrated lower-body strength.

joint_resilience.rationale: Meaningful posterior-knee and hamstring tolerance builder under controlled loading, but less broad than integrated lower-body resilience work.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Very low athletic-transfer contribution because the task is supported and isolates knee flexion without gait, balance, or hip-knee coordination.

control.rationale: The machine constrains almost everything; the user mainly controls tempo, pelvis position, and ankle position.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local hamstring stimulus with low systemic fatigue and little unrelated recovery cost.

setup.rationale: Low setup once the machine is available, but pad fit, machine availability, and reproducible body position still matter.

ease.rationale: Easy guided pattern with minimal balance demand, limited mainly by knee-axis alignment, pad position, and controlled range.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are easy to track, with deductions for machine-specific geometry, stack increments, and pad setup.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the machine pad, torso position, and guided lever path.

primary.name: Biceps femoris
primary.evidenceShort: Direct lying/prone leg-curl EMG and MRI support biceps femoris involvement.
primary.evidence: Direct lying and prone leg-curl studies measured lateral hamstrings or biceps femoris long-head activity, and MRI training evidence showed biceps femoris long- and short-head adaptation after prone leg-curl training. It is classified as a primary knee-flexion target.

primary.name: Semitendinosus
primary.evidenceShort: Direct prone leg-curl EMG supports high semitendinosus activity.
primary.evidence: High-density and conventional EMG studies directly measured semitendinosus activity during prone or lying leg-curl conditions, with leg-curl variants producing high hamstring activity and meaningful medial-hamstring involvement.

primary.name: Semimembranosus
primary.evidenceShort: Prone leg-curl MRI supports biarticular medial-hamstring adaptation.
primary.evidence: Semimembranosus is included conservatively from MRI evidence showing prone leg-curl training increased biarticular hamstring muscle volume, including semimembranosus. It is not isolated by the surface EMG studies, so the role relies primarily on MRI and knee-flexion biomechanics.

secondary.name: Gastrocnemius
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured prone leg-curl knee-flexion assistant.
secondary.evidence: A prone leg-curl study measured gastrocnemius lateralis activity during knee-flexion contractions and evaluated how ankle and knee position affected force and activation. It is classified as a secondary assistant, not the intended hamstring target.

evidence.verdict: Prone machine knee-flexion leg curl: biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus primary; gastrocnemius secondary; no separate support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, while MRI training studies estimate adaptation; neither alone proves hypertrophy, mechanical tension, injury risk, or best programming.
evidence.limitsShort: Machine geometry, hip angle, knee angle, ankle position, range of motion, load, tempo, unilateral versus bilateral setup, and seated versus prone position can shift emphasis.
evidence.summary: The lying machine leg curl is classified as a supported knee-flexion isolation exercise for the hamstrings. Direct lying and prone leg-curl EMG supports high biceps femoris and semitendinosus involvement, with lying leg curl showing high hamstring-to-quadriceps activation relative to other lower-body exercises. MRI training evidence supports semimembranosus inclusion because prone leg-curl training increased biarticular hamstring muscle volume. Gastrocnemius is visible as a secondary role because it was directly measured during prone leg-curl contractions and can assist knee flexion, especially as ankle position changes its mechanical contribution.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface EMG, high-density EMG, and MRI answer different questions. EMG is condition-specific excitation data affected by electrode placement, normalization, contraction mode, and load; MRI volume and T2 data provide adaptation or muscle-damage context but do not identify every acute force contributor.
evidence.limitations: Several useful studies used prone leg curls, lying leg curls, or band/manual prone knee flexion rather than one standardized commercial lying machine. Surface EMG evidence is strongest for biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus; semimembranosus is included mainly from MRI training data, not isolated surface EMG. Prone leg curls train the biarticular hamstrings at shorter lengths than seated leg curls, and Maeo et al. found greater hypertrophy after seated versus prone training for the biarticular hamstrings. Local BodyParts3D mappings are now available for biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and gastrocnemius.

studies.finding: Lying leg curl produced greater normalized mean activation of lower lateral and lower medial hamstrings than stiff-legged deadlift in trained men.
studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Contreras B, Tiryaki-Sonmez G, Wilson JM, Kolber MJ, Peterson MD. Regional differences in muscle activation during hamstrings exercise. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2015;29(1):159-164. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000000598.
studies.relevance: Direct lying leg-curl EMG in resistance-trained men using an 8RM load; supports hamstring primary classification and regional-emphasis limitations.

studies.shortCitation: Hegyi et al., Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2019
studies.finding: Prone leg curl was among the exercises with high hamstring activity, and high-density EMG showed exercise-dependent biceps femoris long-head and semitendinosus regional patterns.
studies.citation: Hegyi A, Csala D, Peter A, Finni T, Cronin NJ. High-density electromyography activity in various hamstring exercises. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2019;29(1):34-43. doi:10.1111/sms.13303.
studies.relevance: Directly included prone leg curl and measured biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus with 15-channel high-density EMG in amateur athletes.

studies.shortCitation: Veeck et al., Res Sports Med, 2024
studies.finding: Lying leg curl produced the greatest hamstring-to-quadriceps activation ratio among parallel squat, Romanian deadlift, hip thrust, lying leg curl, and seated knee extension, with relatively homogeneous lateral-to-medial hamstring activation.
studies.citation: Veeck F, de Vargas JS, Godinho RAT, Wilhelm EN, Daros Pinto M, Pinto RS. Hamstring-to-quadriceps activation ratio during lower-limb strengthening exercises. Research in Sports Medicine. 2024;32(5):843-856. doi:10.1080/15438627.2023.2286355.
studies.relevance: Directly studied lying leg curl among common lower-body exercises and supports its high hamstring targeting with low quadriceps contribution.

studies.type: Seated versus prone leg-curl MRI training study
studies.shortCitation: Maeo et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2021
studies.finding: Both seated and prone leg-curl training increased hamstring muscle volume, but seated training produced greater hypertrophy in the biarticular hamstrings because they operated at longer muscle lengths.
studies.citation: Maeo S, Huang M, Wu Y, Sakurai H, Kusagawa Y, Sugiyama T, Kanehisa H, Isaka T. Greater Hamstrings Muscle Hypertrophy but Similar Damage Protection after Training at Long versus Short Muscle Lengths. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2021;53(4):825-837. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002523.
studies.relevance: Direct prone leg-curl training comparison with MRI-measured individual hamstring muscle volume and T2; supports semimembranosus inclusion and seated-versus-prone limitations.

studies.type: Prone leg-curl EMG and EMG-rise study
studies.finding: Conventional prone leg curls at 8, 16, and 24RM produced substantial biceps femoris long-head and semitendinosus peak nEMG, while Nordic hamstring produced faster EMG rise.
studies.citation: Krommes K, Jakobsen MD, Bandholm T, Andersen LL, Zebis MK, Shield AJ, Holmich P, Thorborg K. Cross-sectional Study of EMG and EMG Rise During Fast and Slow Hamstring Exercises. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2021;16(4):1033-1042. doi:10.26603/001c.25364.
studies.relevance: Close prone knee-flexion evidence using an elastic-band leg-curl setup; useful for biceps femoris long-head and semitendinosus activation and fatigue interpretation.

studies.type: Prone leg-curl knee and ankle position EMG
studies.finding: In trained men, prone leg-curl maximal isometric contractions measured biceps femoris, gastrocnemius lateralis, and soleus lateralis activity, with force and activation affected by knee and ankle position.
studies.citation: Marchetti PH, Magalhaes RA, Gomes WA, da Silva JJ, Stecyk SD, Whiting WC. Different Knee and Ankle Positions Affect Force and Muscle Activation During Prone Leg Curl in Trained Subjects. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2021;35(12):3322-3326. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003333.
studies.relevance: Direct prone leg-curl evidence measuring biceps femoris and gastrocnemius lateralis; supports gastrocnemius as a secondary knee-flexion assistant and ankle-position limitations.

movements.name: Parallel Bar Dip
movements.variant: Bodyweight parallel-bar dip performed on fixed parallel or V-shaped dip bars without external load or machine assistance.
movements.description: Support the body on parallel bars with arms straight, shoulders controlled, and the torso slightly inclined as needed. Lower under control by bending the elbows and allowing the shoulders to extend until reaching a manageable depth, then press back up by extending the elbows and flexing the shoulders without collapsing into the bottom position or shrugging at the top.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong bodyweight loading for pectoralis major and triceps brachii, but shoulder depth tolerance, relative strength, and technique can limit target-muscle volume.

strength.rationale: Useful upper-body pushing strength builder, especially once weighted, but bodyweight entry demands and loading setup make force expression less clean than barbell pressing.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build controlled shoulder, elbow, and scapular tolerance, but loaded shoulder extension is a meaningful constraint and is not ideal for every shoulder.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Good upper-body support-strength transfer for calisthenics and obstacle-style tasks, though it remains bilateral and equipment-specific.

control.rationale: Requires meaningful scapular depression, shoulder position, elbow path, depth, and suspended-body control.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Delivers a lot of pressing stimulus with little setup, but high relative load, shoulder-range demands, and failure risk can leak fatigue.

setup.rationale: Needs only a stable dip station or parallel bars, but bar spacing, height, access, and weighted progression setup add friction.

ease.rationale: Simple to understand but hard to perform well because adequate relative strength, shoulder extension tolerance, and scapular control are required from the start.

progression.rationale: Progresses well with a belt, vest, bands, or assistance, but load changes are less granular and less standardized than a stack, dumbbells, or a barbell.

support.rationale: The bars are fixed, but the body is suspended and the user must stabilize the shoulders, scapulae, elbows, trunk, and depth.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: Direct bar-dip EMG supports strong pectoralis loading.
primary.evidence: Direct dip-variation EMG measured pectoralis major during bar dips and found higher peak activation than the bench dip; a separate bar-dip fatigue study found pectoralis major peak activation increased under fatigue and concluded the bar dip effectively targets pectoralis major.

primary.name: Triceps brachii
primary.evidenceShort: Direct bar-dip EMG supports high elbow-extension demand.
primary.evidence: Direct bar-dip EMG measured triceps brachii as a suspected elbow-extension agonist, with higher peak activation than the bench dip. The fatigue study reported increased triceps brachii peak activation when fatigued and concluded the bar dip effectively targets triceps brachii.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-flexion assistant in bar dips.
secondary.evidence: The dip-variation EMG study measured anterior deltoid as a suspected shoulder-flexion agonist and found higher peak activation in the bar dip than in the bench dip. It is secondary because the strongest exact-variant conclusions emphasize pectoralis major and triceps brachii as the main targets.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Measured scapular support demand during bar dips.
support.evidence: Direct dip EMG classified serratus anterior among active scapular stabilizers, with higher peak activation in the bar dip than the bench dip. In the fatigue study, serratus anterior peak activation increased, supporting a visible scapular-support role.

support.name: Latissimus dorsi
support.evidenceShort: Measured stabilizer/depressor contribution in bar dips.
support.evidence: The direct dip studies measured latissimus dorsi as a suspected glenohumeral stabilizer. Bar dips produced higher latissimus activation than bench dips, and the fatigue study reported increased latissimus dorsi peak amplitude among muscles associated with scapular depression.

evidence.verdict: Bodyweight parallel-bar dip: pectoralis major and triceps brachii primary; anterior deltoid secondary; serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Torso lean, bar spacing, shoulder depth, fatigue, added load, assistance, ring instability, and bench-dip substitutions can materially change muscle contribution and shoulder loading.
evidence.summary: The parallel bar dip is classified as a bodyweight upper-body pushing exercise using fixed bars. Direct dip EMG and kinematic evidence supports pectoralis major and triceps brachii as the clearest main targets for a neutral bar-dip entry. Anterior deltoid is included as a measured shoulder-flexion assistant. Serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi are included as support because the direct studies measured them as scapular or glenohumeral stabilizers and reported meaningful activation in the bar-dip condition, especially with fatigue.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation under a specific technique, load, and normalization method. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk. The main direct studies used experienced healthy males and self-selected bar-dip technique.
evidence.limitations: The closest direct studies used a V-shaped bar and self-moderated depth rather than enforcing a single parallel-bar spacing or torso angle. Lower trapezius was measured and increased under fatigue, but it is not shown as a visible role because the local anatomy label groups middle and lower fibers and the concise app classification is clearer with serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi as support. Infraspinatus, biceps brachii, and upper trapezius were not included because their bar-dip evidence is weaker or less directly tied to the main classification. Weighted dips, assisted dips, ring dips, bench dips, and straight-bar dips should be separate movements.

studies.type: Bench, bar, and ring dip EMG and kinematics
studies.finding: Experienced males performed bench, bar, and ring dips; bar dips showed higher peak activation than bench dips for pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, triceps brachii, serratus anterior, and latissimus dorsi.
