studies.shortCitation: Larsen et al., J Sports Sci, 2025
studies.finding: Twenty-two untrained men completed 10 weeks of unilateral leg-extension training; both 90 degree and 40 degree hip-flexion conditions trained rectus femoris and vastus lateralis, with greater rectus femoris hypertrophy in the lower hip-flexion condition.
studies.citation: Larsen S, Sandvik Kristiansen BS, Swinton PA, Wolf M, Fredriksen AB, Falch HN, van den Tillaar R, Sandberg NO. The effects of hip flexion angle on quadriceps femoris muscle hypertrophy in the leg extension exercise. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2025;43(2):210-221. doi:10.1080/02640414.2024.2444713.
studies.relevance: Direct leg-extension training evidence including an upright seated 90 degree hip-flexion condition, with ultrasound outcomes for rectus femoris and vastus lateralis.

studies.finding: Eight weeks of unilateral seated leg-extension training increased rectus femoris and vastus lateralis muscle thickness and knee-extension strength in recreationally active young men.
studies.citation: Varovic D, Zganjer K, Vuk S, Schoenfeld BJ. Drop-Set Training Elicits Differential Increases in Non-Uniform Hypertrophy of the Quadriceps in Leg Extension Exercise. Sports. 2021;9(9):119. doi:10.3390/sports9090119.
studies.relevance: Direct seated leg-extension training evidence for quadriceps hypertrophy and knee-extension strength adaptation.

studies.type: Open-chain knee-extension versus squat hypertrophy study
studies.finding: Eight weeks of unilateral open-chain knee-extension training increased quadriceps volume similarly to closed-chain squat training but produced a different, more distal hypertrophy pattern.
studies.citation: Earp JE, Angelino D, Hatfield DL, Colantuono V, Jackson ER, Morgan KD, Adami A, Melanson KJ, Blazevich AJ. Differing hypertrophy patterns from open and closed kinetic chain training affect quadriceps femoris center of mass and moment of inertia. Frontiers in Physiology. 2023;14:1074705. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1074705.
studies.relevance: Direct open-chain knee-extension training evidence for quadriceps volume adaptation and regional hypertrophy pattern.

studies.shortCitation: Escamilla et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 1998
studies.finding: Open-chain knee extension produced distinct knee extensor torque, muscle activity, and knee joint force patterns compared with squat and leg press tasks.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Fleisig GS, Zheng N, Barrentine SW, Wilk KE, Andrews JR. Biomechanics of the knee during closed kinetic chain and open kinetic chain exercises. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 1998;30(4):556-569. doi:10.1097/00005768-199804000-00014.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics source for open-chain knee-extension joint loading, rehabilitation/training limits, and joint-resilience scoring.

movements.name: Standing Barbell Overhead Press
movements.variant: Standing free-weight barbell overhead press from shoulder or clavicle height, performed as a strict press without leg drive.
movements.description: Stand with the bar at the front of the shoulders or upper chest, hands just outside shoulder width, wrists stacked over the elbows, and ribs braced over the pelvis; press the bar up while moving the head back just enough for a close bar path, finish with the bar over the shoulder joints and elbows extended, then lower under control to the starting position without using the legs.

hypertrophy.rationale: Useful shoulder and triceps hypertrophy stimulus, but balance, bracing, and fatigue can limit targeted local loading.

strength.rationale: Strong vertical pressing strength anchor with clear barbell loading and high force demand.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build shoulder and trunk tolerance when well dosed, but overhead mobility and irritation risk make it less universally resilience-positive.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Meaningful transfer from standing force production, trunk bracing, and overhead control, though it remains bilateral and stationary.

control.rationale: High control demand from overhead bar path, bracing, rib/pelvis position, shoulder rotation, and balance.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low-to-moderate efficiency because systemic bracing, shoulder fatigue, and technical failure can accumulate before target stimulus is maximized.

setup.rationale: Requires barbell setup, rack height or clean-to-start, plates, and enough overhead space.

ease.rationale: Technically demanding because mobility, bar path, bracing, head position, and overhead lockout must be coordinated.

progression.rationale: Barbell loading is measurable, but small jumps, technical sensitivity, and overhead fatigue make progression less smooth than bench or machines.

support.rationale: Very little external support; the user stabilizes the load while standing under a free bar path.

primary.name: Anterior deltoid
primary.evidenceShort: Direct shoulder-press EMG supports major deltoid involvement.
primary.evidence: Standing barbell shoulder press EMG directly measures anterior deltoid activity, and front barbell military press EMG supports anterior deltoid involvement in the close overhead-press family. Medial deltoid is also important in the literature, but it is not available as a visible shared anatomy entry in this dataset.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Elbow-extension contributor in direct shoulder-press EMG.
secondary.evidence: The triceps brachii is directly measured during standing and seated barbell shoulder press variants and contributes to the elbow-extension component of the overhead press.

secondary.name: Pectoralis major
secondary.evidenceShort: Clavicular pec assists the front overhead press.
secondary.evidence: Front barbell military press EMG shows greater pectoralis major excitation than behind-the-neck pressing, and overhead-press mechanics describe the clavicular pectoralis major as assisting the initial shoulder-flexion phase. It is classified as secondary, not the intended target.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Scapular upward-rotation support during overhead pressing.
support.evidence: Military-press EMG reports high serratus anterior involvement, and overhead-press/shoulder-elevation literature supports serratus anterior as a scapular upward-rotation and stabilization muscle rather than a primary pressing target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Biomechanical inference for glenohumeral stabilization.
support.evidence: This support role is an explicit biomechanics inference: shoulder exercise review evidence describes the rotator cuff as stabilizing the glenohumeral joint and controlling humeral head translation during elevation, which is required in an unsupported overhead press.

evidence.verdict: Standing strict barbell overhead press: anterior deltoid primary; triceps brachii and pectoralis major secondary; serratus anterior and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Direct exact evidence is limited; stance, grip, bar path, back support, load, range of motion, and press-from-front vs behind-neck variations change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The standing barbell overhead press is classified as an unsupported free-weight vertical pressing exercise. Direct standing shoulder-press EMG supports deltoid and triceps involvement, while front barbell military press evidence supports a meaningful clavicular pectoralis major contribution. Serratus anterior is included as scapular support from military-press and overhead-press evidence. Rotator cuff inclusion is an explicit biomechanics inference from shoulder-elevation stability literature, not a direct standing barbell overhead-press EMG measurement.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation under a specific exercise setup. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: The best exact study for this entry measured standing and seated shoulder presses with barbells and dumbbells, but it did not measure pectoralis major, serratus anterior, trapezius, or rotator cuff. Some supporting evidence uses seated front barbell military press, light military-press variants, seated dumbbell/kettlebell overhead press, or general shoulder-elevation review evidence. Medial deltoid and upper trapezius are important in the literature but are not visible anatomy entries in this dataset.

studies.type: Standing and seated shoulder press EMG and 1RM comparison
studies.finding: Compared seated and standing barbell and dumbbell shoulder presses and measured anterior, medial, and posterior deltoids plus biceps and triceps brachii.
studies.citation: Saeterbakken AH, Fimland MS. Effects of Body Position and Loading Modality on Muscle Activity and Strength in Shoulder Presses. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2013;27(7):1824-1831. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e318276b873.
studies.relevance: Most direct evidence for the requested standing barbell shoulder press variant; supports anterior deltoid and triceps roles and informs stability/progression scoring.

studies.type: Front/back barbell and machine overhead press EMG
studies.finding: Front barbell military press from the upper chest measured anterior, medial, and posterior deltoid, upper trapezius, pectoralis major, and triceps brachii.
studies.citation: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Esposito F, Ce E. Front vs Back and Barbell vs Machine Overhead Press: An Electromyographic Analysis and Implications For Resistance Training. Frontiers in Physiology. 2022;13:825880. doi:10.3389/fphys.2022.825880.
studies.relevance: Close barbell military press evidence from shoulder/chest height; useful for anterior deltoid, triceps, pectoralis major, barbell-vs-machine, and front-vs-behind-neck interpretation.

studies.type: Military press serratus and trapezius EMG
studies.shortCitation: Bull et al., Electromyogr Clin Neurophysiol, 2001
studies.finding: Military press variants with open and middle grip showed high to very high trapezius and serratus anterior activity.
studies.citation: Bull ML, Vitti M, Freitas V, Rosa GJ. Electromyographic validation of the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles in military press exercises with open and middle grip. Electromyography and Clinical Neurophysiology. 2001;41(4):203-207. PMID:11441637.
studies.relevance: Direct military-press evidence for serratus anterior involvement, though the reported variants and loading differ from a modern loaded strict standing barbell press.

studies.type: Overhead press shoulder and back EMG
studies.finding: Seated one-arm dumbbell and kettlebell overhead press measured anterior deltoid, posterior deltoid, trapezius, serratus anterior, and spinal erectors.
studies.citation: Blazkiewicz M, Hadamus A. The Effect of the Weight and Type of Equipment on Shoulder and Back Muscle Activity in Surface Electromyography during the Overhead Press-Preliminary Report. Sensors. 2022;22(24):9762. doi:10.3390/s22249762.
studies.relevance: Close overhead-press evidence supporting serratus anterior and shoulder-girdle support demands; less direct because it used seated unilateral dumbbell/kettlebell pressing rather than standing barbell pressing.

studies.type: Shoulder muscle activity and function review
studies.finding: Review describes rotator cuff functions in shoulder exercise and serratus anterior contribution to scapular upward rotation, posterior tilt, and stabilization.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Yamashiro K, Paulos L, Andrews JR. Shoulder muscle activity and function in common shoulder rehabilitation exercises. Sports Medicine. 2009;39(8):663-685. doi:10.2165/00007256-200939080-00004.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics and EMG review evidence for glenohumeral and scapulothoracic support roles during arm elevation; used as inference support rather than exact standing barbell press evidence.

studies.finding: Review characterizes the standing press as a complex multi-joint movement using upper-body muscles while the trunk and lower body provide stability.
studies.citation: Soriano MA, Suchomel TJ, Comfort P. Weightlifting Overhead Pressing Derivatives: A Review of the Literature. Sports Medicine. 2019;49:867-885. doi:10.1007/s40279-019-01096-8.
studies.relevance: Supports rating judgments around coordination, balance, setup, progression, and limitations for standing overhead pressing derivatives.

movements.name: Standing Calf Raise
movements.variant: Standing heel raise or plantar-flexion pattern with the knees mostly extended; not the guided standing calf-raise machine.
movements.description: Stand tall with the balls of the feet on the floor or a small edge, keep the knees mostly straight without locking them, rise onto the toes as high as controlled, pause briefly, then lower slowly until the calves are stretched before the next rep.

hypertrophy.rationale: Good direct calf stimulus, especially for gastrocnemius in the standing knee-extended position, but load can be limited without machine or external weight.

strength.rationale: Builds plantar-flexion force, but the bodyweight version is not a high-force global strength anchor.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful ankle and Achilles tendon exposure when loaded through controlled range, but narrower than full lower-body resilience movements.

athletic_transfer.rationale: The ankle action is relevant to gait and jumping, but the slow bilateral standing raise has low coordination and sport-transfer breadth.

control.rationale: Low motor-control demand unless performed single-leg or without hand support.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local calf stimulus with low systemic fatigue and low unrelated recovery cost.

setup.rationale: Very low setup friction because it requires only standing space, optionally an edge or stable support.

ease.rationale: Simple movement pattern with low skill demand, limited mainly by range control and avoiding bouncing.

progression.rationale: Reps are easy to progress, but load progression is limited unless external weight or a machine is introduced.

support.rationale: External support is optional and minimal; the user usually controls balance and ankle path.

primary.name: Gastrocnemius
primary.evidenceShort: Standing calf-raise training preferentially grows gastrocnemius.
primary.evidence: Standing calf-raise training evidence supports greater gastrocnemius hypertrophy than seated calf raises, consistent with the knee-extended plantar-flexion role.

secondary.name: Soleus
secondary.evidenceShort: Soleus contributes to plantar flexion but is less standing-biased than gastrocnemius.
secondary.evidence: Plantar-flexor activation evidence supports soleus contribution during calf-raise tasks, but the standing knee-extended setup is classified here as gastrocnemius-biased.

evidence.verdict: Standing calf raise: gastrocnemius primary; soleus secondary; no separate visible support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG and hypertrophy studies answer different questions; neither directly determines long-term programming by itself.
evidence.limitsShort: Knee angle, single-leg versus double-leg execution, heel deficit, tempo, external load, and machine support change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The standing calf raise is classified as a simple plantar-flexion exercise. The knee-extended standing position supports a gastrocnemius-biased classification with soleus as a meaningful secondary plantar flexor.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Muscle activation and hypertrophy evidence should be interpreted with setup details, especially knee angle and loading method.
evidence.limitations: This entry is not the standing calf-raise machine. A guided machine version would score higher for progression and support and should be a separate movement.

studies.type: Standing versus seated calf-raise hypertrophy study
studies.finding: Triceps surae hypertrophy was greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training.
studies.citation: Nunes JP, et al. Triceps surae muscle hypertrophy is greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training. Frontiers in Physiology. 2023;14:1272106. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1272106.
studies.relevance: Direct standing/seated calf-raise training comparison for calf muscle emphasis.

studies.finding: Multi- and single-joint resistance exercises promoted similar plantar-flexor activation in resistance-trained men.
studies.citation: Multi- and Single-Joint Resistance Exercises Promote Similar Plantar Flexor Activation in Resistance Trained Men. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2020;17(24):9487. doi:10.3390/ijerph17249487.
studies.relevance: Supports gastrocnemius and soleus activation in plantar-flexor resistance exercise.

studies.finding: Combined functional MRI and EMG characterized neuromuscular activation of the triceps surae.
studies.citation: Kinugasa R, Kawakami Y, Fukunaga T. Neuromuscular activation of triceps surae using muscle functional MRI and EMG. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2005;37(4):593-598. doi:10.1249/01.mss.0000159026.99792.76.
studies.relevance: Supports treating gastrocnemius and soleus as triceps-surae contributors rather than one generic calf label.
